title: Design a Ride-Hailing System
summary: Match a rider to a nearby driver in seconds, on top of a live location feed — the real difficulty is the matching-and-pricing loop, not finding nearby drivers.

slides.markdown:
The ask: a rider taps "request ride," and within seconds gets matched to a nearby driver who is actually available and actually heading in a useful direction.

It looks like a proximity-search problem — "find nearby drivers" — but the hard part is everything downstream of the search: scoring candidates fairly, committing one match before the driver gets offered to someone else, and pricing the marketplace so supply and demand don't collapse during a spike.

Treat this as a live, continuously-updating auction with a latency budget measured in seconds, not a static lookup.

**Functional:** a rider requests a ride from A to B; the system matches them with an available driver; either party can cancel before pickup; the fare adjusts for demand via surge pricing.

**Non-functional:** match latency in the single-digit seconds even in a dense city; graceful cancellation handling that doesn't strand either party mid-match; surge fairness — the multiplier should track real local scarcity, not be gameable by a few drivers going offline together.

The tension to name up front: fast matching (grab whoever's closest, now) can conflict with marketplace-wide efficiency (holding out half a second longer might produce much better matches for everyone).

slides.sectionTitle: Back-of-envelope: pings, rides, and matches per second
slides.markdown:
A dense city might have 100,000 active drivers, each pinging location every 4 seconds — that's 25,000 location writes/sec from location updates alone, before a single ride is requested. Concurrent active rides in a metro area can run into the tens of thousands during peak hours.

Matches/sec during a normal evening might be a few hundred; during a demand spike (a concert letting out, a rainstorm) it can spike 10-20x in one neighborhood in minutes. The location-ping volume dwarfs the ride-request volume by orders of magnitude — which is why the location feed needs its own high-write-throughput store, separate from the transactional ride/trip data.

Three calls anchor the flow:

- `requestRide(riderId, pickup, dropoff)` — kicks off matching; returns a match or a short wait.
- `driverLocationUpdate(driverId, lat, lng, heading)` — a continuous, high-frequency stream from every online driver, feeding the location index.
- `acceptMatch(matchId)` — the driver's confirmation; until this fires, the rider isn't committed to that driver, and the driver isn't removed from the candidate pool for anyone else.

Notice the asymmetry: `driverLocationUpdate` is by far the highest-volume call and the one that must never block on anything slow — it just needs to land in the location index fast and often.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: live driver locations vs durable ride records
slides.markdown:
| | Live driver locations | Ride/trip records |
|---|---|---|
| Update rate | Every few seconds, per driver — extremely high write volume | A handful of state changes per ride (requested, matched, started, completed) |
| Durability need | Ephemeral — only the latest position matters, history is disposable | Durable — needed for billing, disputes, support, analytics |
| Right store | In-memory geospatial index (e.g. a geohash-backed cache) | A transactional database with real persistence guarantees |
| Failure cost | Losing a few seconds of a stale position is a minor UX hit | Losing a trip record is a billing/compliance problem |

**How to decide:** these two datasets have opposite durability and volume profiles, so forcing them into one store either overpays for durability on the location feed or underpays for it on trip records — split them from day one.

![Ride-hailing architecture: location, matching, trip, and pricing services with requestRide flowing through the matching engine](assets/architecture-overview.svg)

Each service has a distinct load and durability profile: the location service is write-heavy and ephemeral, the matching engine is CPU-bound and stateless per request, the trip service is the durable system of record, and pricing runs its own aggregation loop over recent supply/demand.

Splitting these lets each scale on its own axis instead of one monolith straining to satisfy all four profiles at once.

slides.sectionTitle: The matching algorithm: nearest-driver vs marketplace efficiency
slides.markdown:
The naive algorithm — offer the ride to whichever available driver is physically closest — is simple and fast, but it's myopic: it can send a driver who's about to finish another trip three streets away while ignoring one who just became free and is a better fit for the *next* request too.

A marketplace-aware matcher looks slightly wider: it considers driver heading (are they already moving toward this pickup?), ETA (not just straight-line distance), and sometimes holds a match decision for a fraction of a second to consider multiple riders and drivers together, so the overall set of matches is better even if any single one isn't the fastest possible.

The trade-off is real: nearest-driver minimizes this rider's wait; marketplace-aware matching minimizes average wait across all riders, at the cost of a small delay per match.

![The match loop: query candidates, offer top candidate, retry next-best on decline, acceptMatch on success](assets/match-loop.svg)

The loop is designed to fail forward: a declined or timed-out offer doesn't restart the whole search, it just advances to the next-ranked candidate from the same scored list.

That's what keeps end-to-end match latency low even when the first-choice driver doesn't respond immediately.

assets.alt: The match loop: query candidates, offer top candidate, retry next-best on decline, acceptMatch on success

slides.markdown:
**Surge pricing** raises the fare multiplier in a zone when demand (open ride requests) outstrips supply (available drivers) there, computed continuously per geographic zone from a rolling window of recent requests and driver availability.

The purpose isn't just extra revenue — it's a signaling mechanism on both sides: a higher price both dampens marginal demand (some riders wait it out) and pulls supply in (drivers in nearby, calmer zones are incentivized to reposition toward the surge). Without it, a demand spike just produces a long queue with no mechanism to relieve it.

The multiplier needs to update fast enough to track a real spike (a stadium emptying) but not so jumpily that it flickers on normal minute-to-minute noise.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: greedy nearest-match vs batched matching
slides.markdown:
| | Greedy nearest-match | Batched matching |
|---|---|---|
| Decision timing | Matches each request the instant a driver is available | Collects requests and drivers over a short window, then matches the whole batch at once |
| Optimizes for | This rider's wait time | Aggregate marketplace efficiency (total distance, total wait) |
| Latency cost | Near-zero added delay | Adds the batch window (often just 1-3 seconds) to match time |
| Best fit | Low-density areas with few simultaneous requests | Dense areas or spikes, where many requests and drivers overlap in time |

**How to decide:** greedy wins where there's rarely more than one plausible match to choose from; batching earns its small added latency exactly when a spike creates enough simultaneous options that a smarter global assignment meaningfully beats first-come-first-served.

slides.sectionTitle: The bottleneck: the matching engine during a demand spike
slides.markdown:
When a concert lets out, thousands of riders in a few square blocks request rides within minutes of each other. The location service and pricing service scale relatively gracefully — they're mostly independent per-zone computations — but the matching engine has to reconcile a sudden, dense many-to-many problem: many riders, a comparatively small pool of nearby drivers, all needing consistent, non-conflicting assignments.

This is exactly where batched matching earns its keep over pure greedy assignment — a short batching window lets the engine solve a better global assignment instead of a stampede of independent nearest-match lookups colliding on the same handful of nearby drivers.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: matching purely by straight-line distance
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The closest driver by GPS distance is always the best match."

**Why it's wrong:** straight-line distance ignores road network reality and driver intent. A driver 200 meters away but heading the opposite direction on a one-way street, or stuck across a river with no nearby bridge, can have a far worse real ETA than a driver 600 meters away who's already moving toward the pickup on the right road.

**Correct model:** score candidates by estimated ETA along the actual road network, factoring in current heading and traffic — not raw distance. A short straight-line distance is a weak proxy for "will arrive soonest," and treating it as the ranking signal produces bad matches that look correct on a map.
